When the raw focal array and its residual share their autocorrelation, the relabelling test holds the nominal level for all three statistics, at covariate correlations up to $0.9$ and in networks of $20$ to $100$ actors. A normal reference rejects a true null at rates up to $0.96$. With sender and receiver effects modelled, every statistic rejects a true null at $0.035$ to $0.070$ in all conditions, and power against a focal effect of $0.10$ rises from at most $32\%$ to at least $99.9\%$. When the actor effects cannot be modelled, adding the sender and receiver means of the nuisance covariates keeps DSP at its level. We give recommendations and illustrate the method on the EIES message-count network.

title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring
summary: Reconstruction of pseudo-individual patient data (pseudo-IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier curves and number-at-risk tables is widely used to support secondary survival analyses when individual-level data are unavailable. However, the reconstruction is generally not unique because the published information does not determine how censoring is distributed within each risk-table interval. We study the non-identifiability that remains after interval-level event and censoring totals have been reconstructed. Different within-interval censoring placements can yield similarly good Kaplan-Meier agreement but different risk-set and censoring patterns, with possible effects on subsequent analyses. We characterize this non-identifiability, introduce a systematic allocation scheme, and assess its impact on reconstructed pseudo-IPD and downstream analyses. Simulation studies were conducted to examine how within-interval censoring allocation affects pseudo-IPD reconstruction under different risk-table resolutions and censoring settings. The proposed approach was also illustrated using published data from CheckMate 067. Our analysis suggests that considering multiple reconstructions provides a practical way to assess the impact of this non-identifiability on downstream analyses.

title: Guarded Readmission Weighting for Robust Single-Index Frechet Regression
summary: Single-index Frechet regression reduces the predictor dimension for metric-space responses such as distributions, networks or curves, but its estimators are sensitive to outliers. We propose guarded readmission weighting (GRW), a one-step computation of case weights from the predictors and the response distances, usable with any weighted estimator. GRW starts from a high-breakdown fit to a multidimensional scaling surrogate, readmits cases by an add-one metric Cook's distance, downweights remote predictors and keeps a response isolation factor in the final weights. If fewer than $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the $n$ cases are replaced, objects far from the uncontaminated responses receive weight zero; under elliptical predictors, weights depending on the predictors only through the index and the Mahalanobis distance keep the population weighted directions in the index subspace. In simulations, three GRW-weighted estimators keep the mean projection distance to the true direction below about 0.5 under up to 30% scattered and 20% clustered bad leverage points, whereas deletion and $α$-distance covariance become much less accurate as contamination grows; $α$-distance covariance is more accurate in most clean, shape-outlier and good-leverage settings. In two applications, under planted contamination, the weighted surrogate-assisted and least squares directions move less than those of methods without GRW.

title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data
summary: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma.

title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis
summary: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

title: Analytical Wald Power for Lagged Coefficients in the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model
summary: In a longitudinal study, the number of participants and the number of waves both affect how much power the study has to detect a lagged effect. The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) is widely used to study within-person dynamics, but existing approaches to power analysis for this model typically rely on simulation or target likelihood-ratio tests. Starting from the likelihood score, we derive analytical Wald power for each lagged coefficient in the bivariate RI-CLPM. Across 30 designs, we compared our analytical results with power estimates from two R packages, powRICLPM for simulated Wald power and semPower for analytical likelihood-ratio power. The mean absolute difference was less than one percentage point in each comparison. By avoiding repeated simulation and model fitting, the analytical method saves time when evaluating power for a target path across many combinations of sample size (N) and number of waves (T).

title: Projection of multidimensional count data IRT models and their empirical indistinguishability
summary: Empirical test data is rarely unidimensional. If one dimension is of interest, projective item-response-theory (IRT) models can be used to work with a unidimensional model without neglecting the multidimensionality of the data. This work extends the projective IRT literature to count data IRT models from the Two-Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model framework. We build on the definition of empirical indistinguishability and analytically derive closed-form expressions for discrimination parameters and item intercepts after projection. The dispersion parameters of the projected Two- Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model are obtained with numerical approximations. The analytical calculations are not limited to the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution. In addition, rotation methods are applied before projection. Results are illustrated and evaluated using empirical data from cognitive ability assessment items and in a simulation study. The projected model performed better in terms of RMSE, Spearman correlation between the true and estimated person parameters, and coverage of 95% confidence intervals based on the Fisher information than an approximation by a standard unidimensional model fitted to multidimensional data. No improvement in bias over the standard unidimensional model, nor improvement across all metrics over the multidimensional model, were observed.

title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit
summary: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

title: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model as a Statistical Model: Identification, Estimation, and Model Comparison
summary: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) distinguishes stable differences between people from lagged associations within individuals. We use a matrix representation to study its statistical properties for p variables measured across T waves. We derive a necessary and sufficient rank condition for global identification when transition matrices and innovation covariances vary by wave. Under time-invariant transitions, the condition specifies when three waves suffice. For complete Gaussian trajectories, matrix differentiation yields the profile likelihood score for each covariance and transition block. We also derive the population parameters of the conventional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) when an RI-CLPM with fixed parameters generates the data. Our formulas quantify how CLPM slopes for observed variables differ from RI-CLPM slopes for within-person deviations at each transition. When the RI-CLPM transition matrix is time-invariant, the comparison also covers CLPM slopes pooled across waves. The formulas recover earlier bivariate results and show when cross-lagged slopes can appear, cancel, reverse sign, or change their ordering across models.

title: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics
summary: Filtering methods are routinely deployed with misspecified state-space models, where Bayesian filters can diverge and become overconfident. Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering is a recent, hyperparameter-free alternative that was demonstrated to outperform (generalised) Bayesian filtering methods when either the dynamical model or the measurement model is structurally misspecified. This can be attributed to \emph{hedging} behaviour: when an observation conflicts with the forecast, the PrO update places mass near both. Yet existing implementations of PrO filtering rely on unimodal (Gaussian) approximations, whose ability to effectively hedge is limited. This paper develops the first nonparametric, particle-based implementation of PrO filtering. The key obstacle, that PrO filtering distributions are only implicitly defined, is overcome by constructing a path from the predictive to the PrO filtering distribution whose rate is available in closed form, enabling the use of kernel mean embedding dynamics for measure transport. The resulting algorithm requires only simulation from the dynamical model and evaluations of the likelihood, with neither importance weights nor the predictive density. Moreover, as we prove, the number of pseudo-time steps it requires does not grow with the outlyingness of the observation, in contrast to transport along the Bayesian tempering path. An empirical assessment shows substantial improvement over Gaussian variation of PrO filtering in challenging nonlinear examples where Gaussian approximation is unreasonably limited.

title: Horseshoe-Type Shrinkage from Ratio-Generated Priors
summary:
We develop a class of horseshoe-type shrinkage priors generated by ratios of independent numerator and denominator random variables. Large denominator values produce concentration near zero, small denominator values generate heavy tails, and the numerator determines scale and geometry and may also influence tail behavior. We establish general origin and tail asymptotics, including power and logarithmic singularities. Under a Gaussian likelihood and regularly varying prior tails, the posterior mean approaches the observation for large signals, with risk approaching that of the unshrunk observation.
  The denominator also induces a latent shrinkage factor. For a Cauchy denominator, this factor has exactly the ${\rm Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ distribution, whatever the numerator. With a Gaussian numerator and appropriate scale calibration, it recovers the classical horseshoe shrinkage coefficient, whereas non-Gaussian numerators can change the effective posterior shrinkage, even in its asymptotic rate.
  The Cauchy/Cauchy prior illustrates the theory, with a logarithmic singularity at the origin in one dimension, power singularities in higher dimensions, and logarithmically modified Cauchy-order tails. Its posterior mean shrinks smoothly, whereas its spatial median behaves nearly as a threshold rule. We also compare the Cauchy/Cauchy posterior mean with fifteen established shrinkage procedures on the four standard Donoho-Johnstone test functions, finding competitive, though not uniformly superior, wavelet-denoising performance.
  The ratio construction generalizes several published shrinkage priors and offers a flexible framework for sparse estimation, with natural applications to wavelet shrinkage, variable selection, and structured multivariate shrinkage.

title: Fairness-Regularized Principal Component Analysis
summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) optimizes aggregate reconstruction accuracy but may represent heterogeneous groups unevenly. We study fairness-regularized PCA, which balances aggregate reconstruction risk against worst-group reconstruction regret, and establish its population and statistical properties. First, we characterize the reconstruction-fairness trade-off and show that, under a nondegeneracy condition, a small fairness penalty reduces worst-group regret to first order while increasing aggregate reconstruction risk only to second order. This reveals a vanishing initial marginal cost of improving fairness. We also identify conditions under which the regularization path remains locally constant. A minimax spectral characterization shows that, under an optimal effective eigengap condition, the convex relaxation is exact and Fair PCA is equivalent to ordinary PCA with endogenously adjusted group weights. Second, we develop a statistical theory for estimating fairness-regularized principal subspaces. A uniform eigengap over the set of possibly nonunique dual optimizers implies polyhedral identification and quadratic growth, yielding first-order perturbation bounds and convergence rates that accommodate growing dimensions, ranks, and numbers of groups. Third, we establish uniform recovery of the reconstruction-fairness path and theoretical guarantees for data-adaptive penalty selection. Simulations and an NHANES accelerometry application demonstrate substantial improvements in worst-group representation quality with minimal loss of aggregate reconstruction accuracy.

title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation
summary: The next German Census (2031) is planned to be the country's first fully register-based census, relying exclusively on administrative data sources. In addition to the population registers, ten further administrative registers are envisaged, covering a wide range of information, from driving licences to agricultural social insurance. This study simulates potential data-quality challenges in linking these registers using quasi-identifiers (QIDs), such as names and dates of birth. Using a synthetic population dataset (N=80,206,770), we systematically vary experimental factors related to register characteristics. Across the 1,458 experimental conditions studied, results vary considerably. Some plausible scenarios range from 500,000 to 1,000,000 false-negative linkage errors per linked register. These findings suggest that implementing an automated register-based census using the currently envisaged registers may prove challenging and could require substantial manual post-processing to achieve acceptable data quality.
